extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsels, press agents, media strategists, and students of public relations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations practitioners on understanding and shaping public opinion via press and other media channels, including how to evaluate media standards, audience predispositions, and interaction between institutions and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: public_opinion_as_aggregate_of_individual_judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion is the aggregate result of individual opinions—now uniform, now conflicting—of the men and women who make up society or any group of society; to understand public opinion one must go back to the individual who makes up the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the 'mental equipment' of the average individual: judgments often adopted dogmatically from parents, teachers, church, social and economic leaders rather than from research; counselling must account for these individual-level sources when designing messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: identify_sources_of_established_beliefs_and_herd_suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many opinions are adopted on authority (parents, teachers, church, social/economic leaders) and through 'herd-suggestions' that form basal conceptions treated as instinctive truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before attempting to change opinion, trace the sources and authorities that underpin an established belief (a priori judgments) so you can address or work around them.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_direct_denunciation_of_beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: It is seldom effective to call names or to attempt to discredit the beliefs themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than attacking beliefs, the counsel must either discredit the old authorities behind those beliefs or create new authorities by articulating a mass opinion in favor of the new view (example: use of group leaders to sponsor controversial plays like 'Damaged Goods').

rubrics_metrics.name: assess_public_opinion_stubbornness_vs_malleability
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the public mind is stubborn or malleable—passive or active—since opinion can be both naturally uniform and subject to change via institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze historical and contemporary cases (e.g., election outcomes despite press opposition, women suffrage success) and consider multiple influences (press, schools, churches, advertising, film, radio) to judge how receptive a given public will be.

rubrics_metrics.name: conform_to_media_standards_'fit_to_print'
rubrics_metrics.description: Media organs have standards (exemplified by the slogan 'All the news that's fit to print') which determine what they will publish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand an outlet's definition of 'fit'—including timeliness, significance, decency, and respect for privacy—and shape submissions so editors see them as meeting those standards; failure to conform will limit pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: newsworthiness_timeliness_and_significance
rubrics_metrics.description: News is defined as anything timely which is significant to newspaper readers in their relations to the community, the state and the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame releases to emphasize timeliness and tangible significance to the outlet's readership; know that 'significant' is often judged by public consensus and the paper's audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: balance_completeness_with_decency_and_privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Completeness in reporting is limited by commonly accepted ideas of decency and by the rights of privacy; editors discriminate between what the public is entitled to know and what an individual may keep private.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing material, anticipate editors' privacy and decency standards and provide necessary context or redactions to increase likelihood of publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: analyze_interaction_between_public_and_media
rubrics_metrics.description: Action and interaction are continually going on between forces projected to the public (press, pulpit, film, radio) and the public itself; institutions both reflect and shape public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the relative powers of channels in a given context and plan messaging that both conforms to the medium's norms and appeals to the public's current understanding; monitor feedback loops.

rubrics_metrics.name: enlist_established_points_of_view_and_authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of any force attempting to modify public opinion depends on its ability to enlist established points of view and authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure endorsements, group leaders, or authoritative sponsors to lend legitimacy to controversial messages (example: using education groups to back a play discussing sex education).

rubrics_metrics.name: coordinate_multi_channel_communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple mediums (press, pulpit, schools, motion pictures, advertising, lectures, radio) in coordination since combined channels can bring about conversion of public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design integrated campaigns that leverage different channels' strengths and target the same underlying beliefs for maximum effect (example: suffrage movement, birth-control education).

rubrics_metrics.name: anticipate_media_constraints_and_censorship_factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Media presentation is often restricted—consciously or unconsciously—by advertiser interests, audience prejudices, and other controlling conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess potential constraints (advertiser preferences, target 'quality public', cultural taboos) and adapt messaging or choose alternative channels to avoid self-censorship or inadequate presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: test_public_opinion_with_trial_balloons_and_monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Public statements and press outputs can be used as 'trial balloons' to test popular reaction; delegates and organizations monitor clippings to gauge public sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use limited releases, trial statements, and systematic clipping/monitoring to measure reactions before committing to a major course of action (example: Hague Conference opening to correspondents and use of clipping bureaus).

rubrics_metrics.name: adapt_to_audience_moral_limitations_and_desire_to_be_pleased
rubrics_metrics.description: Media and spokespeople often adapt their messaging to please the crowd and to the moral limitations of their clients/audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame persuasive content so it will be acceptable to the outlet’s readership and moral sensibilities; sensational or confrontational tactics risk alienating the audience and editors (Mencken/ Pulitizer observations).

rubrics_metrics.name: use_public_figures_and_trust_building_measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations appoint prominent public figures or respected directors to their activities to assure the public of honest and socially-minded conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ well-known, trusted individuals as spokespeople or board members to increase public confidence and media receptivity (examples: Franklin Roosevelts, Will Hays).

rubrics_metrics.name: selective_reporting_to_maintain_public_morale
rubrics_metrics.description: In times of stress a newspaper may see a duty to perform in keeping up the morale of the community and may exercise selective action in reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, account for community morale considerations in timing and tone of releases; proposing helpful, morale-boosting angles may increase editorial support.
